Research in multilingual information retrieval and machine translation has shown the challenges of implementing natural language processing technologies across languages (Casacuberta and Marino, 2018), particularly recognizing that an approach suitable for one language may not be effective when translated to another. In many cases, developing a sentiment classifier in a particular language results in an in-explicit linguistic model of the language. That is, even though the classifier might be a deep learning model and perform well, the very fact that we require to translate text from that language into English to do training, means that the classifier will heavily rely upon linguistic patterns in English rather than in the target language. Furthermore, another challenge is the intrinsic cross-lingual sentiment discrepancy, as sentiment may be expressed differently in different languages. In this work we modify this traditional two step approach by, in addition to relying on high-dimensional vector embeddings, augmenting our training corpus by polar words although containing extremely little linguistic information provide highly informative instances for learning such discrepancy in sentiment. response: Generating concise and coherent summaries from a single document is an essential task in natural language processing. Although various methods have been proposed to tackle this problem, effective summarization methods are still challenging to design. One major obstacle hindering current summarization methods is that most previous models relied heavily on shallow models and overlooked the complexity of coherence in a summary. To group together sentences that share strong semantic relationships, it is ideal if the model can capture the structural coherence of the summary. Another potential problem is that most models do not incorporate sentence compression into the summarization process. The process of sentence compression can bring significant improvement to the quality of the generated summaries because it relieves the problem of information explosion in a summary. Traditionally, hidden Markov models (HMM) have been widely used for language modeling and pattern recognition tasks due to their ability to capture the probabilistic relationships between states by modeling the transition probabilities and emission distributions. However, the standard HMM is limited to modeling single segment units with fixed length. To model the sequence of arbitrarily length segments in order to capture coherent document structures and clause levels, the hidden semi-Markov model (HSMM) becomes the ideal choice. It models the relevant segment variables, duration variable for each segment, thus allowing for disorder in the segments. Furthermore, another key point of HSMM is that it elucidates sentences as segments, solved the defects of former mentioned methods which may generate disjointed results. Even though the HSMM offers some advantages such as high accuracy and the ability to model complex structures, there are limited applications for HSMM in summarization. Stance encompasses a range of evaluations, including beliefs, attitudes, and opinions (Biber and Jones, 2000). As Knutson (2014) pointed out, accurately classifying stance is crucial for effective analysis and criticism of arguments. response: Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks often involve complex linguistic structures and rules. Many tasks, such as part-of-speech (POS) tagging, dependency parsing, and Chinese word segmentation, have both syntactic and semantic aspects that need to be considered. While probabilistic models have been highly effective in NLP, they often rely on weakly-informed heuristics, and suffer from the related issues of sparsity and lack of robustness (Chen and Goodman, 1999). In this work, we investigate the role of deterministic constraints in NLP tasks, and how these can be learned and efficiently applied to improve model performance. Our study spans two tasks: English POS tagging and Chinese word segmentation. POS tagging is a core NLP task that aims to assign a POS label to each token in a sentence. For instance, given the word "running", the task is to determine whether it is a verb, noun, or other part of speech. Chinese word segmentation is a variant of POS tagging, where the goal is to split a Chinese word into its constituent parts. This task has the additional challenge of dealing with the complexities of the Chinese language, such as homophonic characters and complex word forms. For both tasks, we show that with proper representation, a large number of deterministic constraints can be learned from training examples. These constraints capture various linguistic properties, including POS syntax, lexical semantics, and character patterns. The challenge of applying learned constraints in a probabilistic framework is to avoid over-reliance on these constraints and maintain model robustness. For the task of English POS tagging, we find that the learned constraints can be directly incorporated into the Viterbi decoding algorithm, significantly improving its efficiency and accuracy. The application of learned constraints in a deterministic framework has the added benefit of inducing sparse models, which in turn speeds up inference and improves testing robustness. This demonstrates that deterministic constraints can effectively aid probabilistic modeling. However, for optimal performance, we find that these constraints are best applied to a word-based model. To incorporate these constraints, we develop an integer linear programming (ILP) formulation that strikes a balance between computational complexity and solution quality. Our empirical results show that the proposed ILP formulation achieves significant improvements over the baseline models, demonstrating the effectiveness of deterministic constraints in word segmentation. By leveraging the distribution of constraints in the data, we are able to learn compact yet powerful representations that not only improve model accuracy but also lead to faster inference times. Our work highlights the importance of deterministic modeling in NLP, and demonstrates that with careful design, learned constraints can be efficiently and effectively applied to complex tasks to achieve significant performance gains. Recently, distantly supervised relation extraction has emerged as an effective approach to scaling relation extraction up to large-scale corpora by leveraging existing knowledge graphs to automatically collect training data [Mintz et al., 2009;Saparov et al., 2019]. Although distantly supervised relation extraction has shown promising results in identifying valid relation instances, it inevitably suffers from the wrong labeling problem [Zeng et al., 2019]. In other words, noisy or incorrect supervision information can significantly affect the performance of distantly supervised relation extraction models, leading to the recognition of a large volume of false positive instances. Many efforts have been devoted to identifying valid instances from noisy data [Krishnamurthy and Finkel, 2018; Jia et al., 2019]. However, the existing methods often focus on refining individual relation instances, disregarding the rich semantic correlations that exist between relations in relevant relation hierarchies. These correlations can help alleviate the risk of obtaining noisy supervision information. By understanding the hierarchical structure of relations, it is possible to gain insight into the relationships between high-level abstract entities and discover long-tail relations composed of lesser-known expressions. Models that can capture such correlations would not only alleviate the noise effect of wrong labels but also yield better generalization ability. In this paper, we incorporate the hierarchical information of relations into distantly supervised relation extraction. Our proposed method employs a novel hierarchical attention scheme to capture the interrelation between relations across different levels in the hierarchy and between entities with specific semantics. Specifically, our model comprises multiple layers of coarse-to-fine attention mechanisms that provide a comprehensive understanding of relations, learning to weigh the importance of individual relation instances based on their relevance to latent high-level relation templates. By leveraging hierarchical attention, our models can effectively adapt to the given supervision information and minimize the noise effect. Moreover, this method allows our model to learn to extract long-tail relations more efficiently than existing approaches. We carry out comprehensive experiments on a large-scale benchmark dataset to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Our results show that the hierarchical relation extraction model outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, validating the importance of capturing hierarchical correlations in relation extraction tasks. The high-quality source code of this paper can be obtained from https://github.com/thunlp/HNRE. Contribution 1: This paper combines the strengths of distantly supervised relation extraction and hierarchical relation attention, distinguishing itself as the first to model hierarchical relation extraction for long-tail relation extraction. Contribution 2: We propose a novel hierarchical attention scheme for capturing rich semantic correlations in relation hierarchies, achieving better noisy-sparse ratio management and boost for long-tail relation extraction. Contribution 3: Our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on a large-scale benchmark dataset. We discuss technical details of the proposed method and the experimental results in Sections 3 and 4, respectively, with the full evaluation methodology and supporting experimental details in Appendix A and B.assistant The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 provides a detailed overview of distantly supervised relation extraction and the motivation behind the motivation of the proposed approach

response: Dependency parsing is a critical component in many Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications, particularly in supporting documentation of a language's syntax and semantics. In linguistics, the term 'syntax' refers to the rules and structures governing how words combine to form phrases and sentences, while 'semantics' pertains to the meaning of language constructs. Field linguistics, where researchers document and study a native speaker's linguistic abilities, involves annotating language samples using dependency parse trees, a way of representing syntactic structure as an unlabeled tree, where each node is a word and its dependencies are represented as edges. However, manually annotating data is an exhaustive, time-consuming, and often expensive process, particularly for languages that lack existing resources. Therefore, developing tools to aid in this process is highly beneficial. Traditional supervised parsing approaches rely heavily on large annotated datasets to learn a set of general rules to apply to new, unseen data. However, in the context of language documentation, it is often the case that the available data is limited and of varying quality. As a result, in this work, we are motivated to investigate incremental learning, an approach to learning that can utilize small amounts of training data to make predictions and continue to update the learned model as additional data becomes available. We propose a design to support field linguists in documenting languages using dependency parsing tools as part of the WordsEye Linguistics Tools (WELT) framework. In many applications, such as opinion mining and emotion detection, it is essential to accurately determine the polarity of a given text to extract meaningful insights. However, the complexity of natural language and the nuances of human expression make this task non-trivial, even for humans. Collocation polarity disambiguation is a specific instance of this problem where the polarity of a word or phrase depends on its co-occurrence with other words, referred to as the target. For example, the word "long" in the sentence "this product has long battery life" is likely to have a positive polarity, whereas in the sentence "the line was long for the movie," the same word is associated with a negative polarity. response: Dependency parsing is a prominent task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), with a wide range of applications in text analysis and information extraction (Sang and Buchholz, 2000;Nivre et al., 2006). One common approach to dependency parsing is scoring a parse via a linear function of a set of indicator features. These features are typically manually constructed from templates that are applied to parts of the parse tree (Collins, 2003). The potential of this approach is significant, as the design of a template-based model allows a trade-off between discriminatory power and model complexity. However, the choice of templates themselves is often based on linguistic intuition (Galbraith et al., 2013), and previous approaches have considered only a small subset of the possible combinations, mainly due to statistical and computational efficiency considerations (Herschenhammer and Roth, 2013). For instance, if a template is defined as "Subject-Verb-Object", it can give rise to features describing "plural subject", "passive verb", and "artificial object", but it cannot be applied to more complex, re-entrant structures. Moreover, the current state of the art models sometimes have high accuracy, especially for languages with relative complexity like English (Durrett and Klein, 2013), but, for very challenging languages, like Czech, the results obtained are still poor. There is therefore a strong need for efficient models that can capture, and learn, the structure and semantics of the parse tree in an automatic and scalable way. In this paper, we address this gap by presenting a novel kernel for dependency parsing. The goal of this kernel is to facilitate efficient parsing with feature representations corresponding to a much larger set of combinations, typically designed by a linguist and implemented manually with heavy computational costs (Nivre, 2008). We call this kernel "Template-Sum-Product Kernel" (TSPK), because it sums over and combines template primitive properties through product operations. response: Automated essay scoring has been a long-standing challenge for researchers and educators. With the rapid growth of educational resources online and the increasing amount of manual grading required, it is more essential than ever to have a computer-based system that can accurately evaluate written essays. Current automated systems for scoring essays rely heavily on hand-crafted features, such as the number of group nouns used or use of the first person, to evaluate student performance. While these features have been shown to be effective, a major limitation is that they do not provide an understanding of the underlying thought process that goes into writing an essay. This reliance on engineered features also makes the use of automated scoring systems tightly bound to the quality of the features chosen, making it even more challenging to improve the performance of such systems. One primary reason for this lack of generalizability is that manual feature engineering approaches impose predefined assumptions about the content and structure of the essays that need to be scored. However, these assumptions may fail to capture the full nuances of human scoring behaviors. For instance, a good essay may contain hypothetical examples or shift in topic mid-sentence, which is difficult to model through engineered features. Inspired by the recent breakthroughs in image and speech recognition, various researchers have attempted to leverage various machine learning techniques, including neural networks, to design more robust and generalizable automatic essay scoring systems. While differentiable neural networks may offer a high degree of flexibility in modeling complex relationships between the input text and assigned score, their ability to learn such relationships from scratch is first and foremost conditional on the type of model and quality of training data used. To bridge the gap between the complexity of human scoring behaviors and the capacity of machine learning models, we investigate a neural approach to automated essay scoring. response: Machine translation (MT) has been a cornerstone of natural language processing (NLP), aimed to automatically translate text from one language to another. The nowadays conventional approach of machine translation involves several key assumptions: (1) that languages are composed of words, and (2) that these words are composed of individual symbols or characters that are manipulated using word-based translation systems. However, the above word-based assumptions may not hold in all languages and scenarios. For instance, in many Asian languages like Chinese and Japanese, words are not separated by any spaces or special characters, instead they form a continuous stream of characters. In order to naturally and accurately process these languages, the notion of a "word" becomes vague. Therefore, studying machine translation through a character-based approach could provide depth and room for language and scenario adaptations that are too hard to explore using existing standard word-based methods. Incorporating character-level alignment techniques into the machine translation process will not only provide the framework for adapting these methods for less common and more challenging languages, but also create opportunities for more general purpose machine translation systems in various non-language related areas. This paper proposes a translation model that does away with the words, using an inversion transduction grammar alignment technique to character strings for training a character-based model. This method represents a major departure from traditional word-based translation models, setting off anew path in NLP for the analysis and processing of languages. There have been many impressive breakthroughs in machine translation in recent years ( Vaswani et al., 2017; Bahdanau et al., 2015; Cho et al., 2014). However, these models are all grounded in the word-uniting worldview: a set of words being translated from a source language into a target language is a sequence of symbols. This perspective is more ontological than others, in the sense that it has been hardwired into the architecture of current machine translation systems: words are atoms, and sequences of words are the sole primitive units of meaning that the systems deal with. In contrast, to the traditional division of NLP into "phrase-based" (equivalent to sentence-based), "syntax-based," and "model-based," we add an additional dimension: remembering that free translation is often possible across the character string boundary. Traditional methods of discourse annotation, relying on expensive and labor-intensive manual annotation, have limited their widespread adoption. In recent years, crowdsourcing has emerged as an effective paradigm to alleviate the annotation burden. With the widespread availability of cheap online labor, a large number of crowd workers can be enlisted to perform various NLP tasks, including discourse annotation. However, despite its potential, discourse annotation still remains a particularly data-hungry task due to its complex nature. Typical discourse annotation tasks require annotators to identify and label various discourse relationships and structures, such as relationships between clauses (e.g., cause-effect) or discourse markers indicating the speaker's intention (e.g., hedging). Due to the subjective and nuanced nature of these tasks, annotators need to have substantial expertise in both linguistics and domain-specific knowledge, making it challenging to recruit and retain high-quality annotators. Domain adaptation (DA) aims to improve the performance of a model on a target domain (or language) using labeled data from a different source domain (or language). Traditional GEC systems relied heavily on rule-based approaches and machine learning techniques, with moderate success on correcting specific types of errors. However, recent advancements in deep learning have led to the development of sophisticated neural machine translation (NMT) models that can capture subtle patterns in language and achieve state-of-the-art performance in machine translation and related tasks. However, word repetition is not always a reliable indicator of topical cohesion, particularly in texts where authors employ stylistic variations or in domains where vocabulary is highly technical or dynamic. Moreover, research in topical segmentation, which involves identifying meaningful segments of a document based on its thematic content, has also highlighted the limitations of relying solely on word repetition. Traditional approaches to topical segmentation rely heavily on lexical features, such as word co-occurrence and word frequency, to detect topical shifts. While these features have proven effective in certain contexts, they may not be sufficient to capture the nuances of topical change, especially in genres where authors often exploit various linguistic devices to signal shifts in topic. For example, in literary narratives, authors frequently employ contradictory statements, ironic remarks, or non-literal language to convey complex themes, making it challenging for word repetition alone to identify topical shifts. They are particularly well suited to formalize the syntax and semantics of programming languages, as well as aspects of natural language processing. A key feature of SCFGs is that they are expressive enough to encode the dependencies and interactions between two parallel string derivations, thereby providing a unified formal framework for both syntax and semantics. In order to fully utilize the potential of SCFGs, a central question is how to extract useful information from them, such as parse trees, semantic meanings and data types. The key to answering this question lies in being able to efficiently compute various probability distributions over derivations and their associated structures, which are crucial for language modeling and parsing tasks. In an SCFG, this probability distribution encodes the likelihood of a derivation, taking into account both the syntactic and semantic aspects of the input string. Prefix probabilities, a variant of the more commonly studied probabilistic context free grammar (PCFG) prefix probabilities, play a crucial role in this endeavor. They measure the probability of a given prefix of a parse tree, taking into account the probability of the other words in the derivation. In this paper, we study the computation of prefix probabilities for SCFGs. Our approach relies on a combination of a novel grammar transformation and standard techniques to bring SCFGs into normal forms. As a byproduct, our formalizations also naturally give rise to new results about prefix probabilities for SCFGs, including the ability to efficiently compute the prefix probabilities of PCFGs and CFGs by restricting the semantics of SCFGs in a specific way. We believe these results have the potential to be a useful tool for understanding various types of probabilistic models found in areas like natural language processing and programming languages. One of the fundamental tools used in structured prediction is the structured perceptron (Collins, 2002), where a perceptron learning rule is applied to structured output space. This has been widely used in various structured learning tasks due to its simplicity, scalability and strong guarantees of convergence. However, in many real-world structured prediction problems, exact inference is often intractable. For instance, in speech recognition and machine translation tasks, calculating the best possible output using an exponential number of potential solutions is impractical and will incur extremely long training time and extremely large memory space usage. One common way to handle this limitation is to rely on approximate inference techniques, where the goal is to find an approximately optimal structured output. Among these methods, beam search (Viterbi, 1967) is one of the most popular techniques in speech recognition and machine translation. response: Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) has emerged as a comprehensive framework for representing the compositional semantics of natural language. Under this framework, individual sentences are annotated with graph-like meaning representations that capture both the syntactic and semantic structure of language. However, completing a comprehensive picture of document-level semantics requires moving beyond the confines of individual sentences. This is particularly important in contexts where texts convey complex, multi-part narratives or discourses. For instance, news articles typically do not convey a single proposition, but rather multiple claims that require drawing certain inferences or relationships between events. The demand for understanding these processes and relationships imposes the need for AMR semantics that operates beyond the single-sentence level. Typical approaches to document-level representation, such as document-level parse trees or the discourse structure of certain theories, lack the depth of representation inherent in AMR graphs. For instance, radiation oncology and pediatrics use distinct jargon and medical terminologies that vary significantly from those used in cardiology or orthopedic surgery. Moreover, even within a single specialty, different physicians may employ unique language and notation styles. As a result, data shortage and the specialist gap present significant challenges to training a broadly applicable medical NER model. Recent advances in deep learning have improved the performance of various natural language processing (NLP) tasks, including NER. In this work, we investigate the problem of cross-specialty medical NER and propose a novel transfer learning framework to alleviate the discrepancy between NER tasks from different domains, including specialty-driven terminological differences. The goal is to design an NER system that, with minimal additional annotations, can be applied across multiple specialties. Our approach to this multi-specialty transfer problem is based on a simple yet effective paradigm: double transfer learning. Concretely, we propose label-aware double transfer learning (La-DTL), which consists of two primary components. response: The evaluation of summarization systems is a crucial task in the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP). Automatic summarization systems have the potential to revolutionize information retrieval and communication, however their performance is heavily dependent on effective evaluation metrics (Nenkova and McKeown, 2011). The Text Analysis Conference (TAC) has been a leading forum for the evaluation of summarization systems since its inception, and the document summarization track has played an integral role in this effort (Durrett, 2012). In the document summarization track of the TAC, evaluation is framed as a ranking problem, where the goal is to rank systems by their ability to select and arrange the most informative content of a set of documents (Dang et al., 2008). One key challenge in this ranking task is in determining a suitable metric for comparison of systems (Fritzinger et al., 2012). To address this challenge, TAC uses a ranking system based on scores from human annotators (Durrett, 2012). This ranking system scores summary systems based on their average score over a collection of document sets, with the top-scoring system declared the winner (Durrett, 2012). However, this approach has some limitations. First, it treats the quality of a summarization system as a single number, which is the average score. This approach does not capture the variability of a system's performance over different document sets. In addition, it does not effectively distinguish between human and machine summarization systems. A human summarizer is expected to produce high-quality summaries regardless of the document set, whereas a machine summarizer may perform well on specific document sets but poorly on others (Kopp and Schwartz, 2012). Moreover, the average score does not provide information on the relative ranking of runs with different average scores (Paass and Eggo, 2013). response: **Introduction** Language models are a crucial component of natural language processing (NLP), particularly in tasks such as machine translation, text summarization, and speech recognition. Traditional n-gram language models, where words are modeled as a consecutive sequence of n items, have been widely used for many years. However, they have several limitations, including the failure to capture long-range dependencies and the inability to generalize to unseen contexts. Recently, there has been a surge of interest in exploring novel approaches to language modeling that can better capture the structure and semantics of language. Given that human languages exhibit a hierarchical and compositional structure, it is natural to ask whether language models can benefit from incorporating this structure into the modeling process. This question is central to the field of syntax and semantics, which aims to assign meaning to words and phrases within an utterance. Recent work in linguistics has shown that the study of syntax and semantics is closely tied to the study of the co-occurrence of words, with syntax and semantics influencing each other in a complex and dynamic way. For example, in English, the verb phrase "cook a fish" conveys a different meaning from the individual words that comprise it, "cook" and "a fish". This meaning is achieved through the arrangement of these words into a specific structure, which reflects their roles in the sentence. In this paper, we introduce Latent Tree Language Model (LTLM), a novel approach to language modeling that encodes syntax and semantics of a given sentence as a tree of word roles. We propose that the nodes in the tree represent specific roles, such as the agent or the patient, while the edges represent the relationships between these roles. We argue that this representation is well-suited to capture the compositional structure of language and to represent long-range dependencies between words. Our proposed model, LTLM, has two key innovations: (a) it incorporates the structure of language into the modeling process through a tree-based representation, and (b) it learns the structure of the tree from the data using a probabilistic framework. The key challenge in developing LTLM is learning a good representation of the tree structure. We address this challenge by proposing two algorithms to infer a tree for a given sentence: a Gibbs sampling algorithm that is fast but may not find the most probable tree, and a dynamic programming algorithm that guarantees to find the most probable tree but is slower. We provide a detailed comparison of the two algorithms and analyze their trade-offs. To evaluate the effectiveness of LTLM, we compare its performance with that of a state-of-the-art n-gram language model, specifically 4-gram Modified Kneser-Ney (MKL). We show that LTLM, when combined with MKL via linear interpolation, achieves significant perplexity reductions (up to 46% for English and 49% for Czech) compared with standalone MKL. Our results demonstrate the potential of LTLM to improve the accuracy of language models in a variety of applications. The rest of this paper is organized as follows: in Section 2, we discuss related work on language modeling and syntax-based language models; in Section 3, we describe the Latent Tree Language Model (LTLM) and its learning phase; in Section 4, we present the two algorithms for inferring a tree for a given sentence; in Section 5, we evaluate the performance of LTLM and compare it with standalone 4-gram Modified Kneser-Ney language model.

Among various sources of parallel data, including manually aligned databases, flameo songs lyrics, and parliamentary debates, the quality and quantity of available corpora vary significantly (Koehn and Knight, 2003;Zapirain et al., 2012). As a result, researchers have turned to mining parallel data from various Web resources, such as Wikipedia, copy-paste Websites, and online forums. Specifically, Web mining data relies on the idea of translating document pairs from corresponding non-parallel but comparable corpora (Koehn, 2005;Lavie et al., 2007). However, this line of work is generally restricted to pre-existing, comparable collections, where the documents are either roughly translated or often similar in content. Thus, several critical issues limit its applicability. First, the quality and efficiency of hypothetical machine translation (HMT) automatically extracting parallel data is typically unknown, since mainstream SMT approaches perform poorly on low-quality parallel training examples (Lavie et al., 2007). Second, current approaches neglect the truth that comparable documents do not always have intrinsic cross-document parallelism (Lavie et al., 2007), potentially resulting in noisy matches and wasted computational resources. In contrast, automatically finding high-quality sentence pairs from the Web would be capable of creating quickly and constantly updated large-scale translation resources by taking advantage of its abundance and rapidly changing landscape. response: Event extraction is a critical task in natural language processing (NLP) with a wide range of applications in text analysis, information retrieval, and knowledge representation. It involves the extraction of structured information about events from unstructured texts, which enables the construction of a comprehensive and accurate event database. Recently, with the rapid growth of social media, extracting events from social media has become an increasingly important task, as it allows for the analysis of current events, trending topics, and public sentiment. However, existing event extractors for social media suffer from several limitations. Firstly, social media messages often lack context due to the informality of the language used. For instance, a tweet like "just got a new job" does not provide sufficient information about the type of job, the company name, or the location of the job. Secondly, the informal nature of social media language often contains jargon, abbreviations, and slang that are difficult for event extractors to comprehend. As a result, existing event extractors may struggle to identify the key elements of an event, such as the participant, location, and time. To address these limitations, mainstream approach for event extraction in social media is to rely solely on relevant features from the social media text, such as named entity recognition (NER) and part-of-speech (POS) tagging. However, these feature-based approaches can be vulnerable to noise and variability in the social media text. Moreover, they may not capture the deeper, contextual relationships between events that are critical for accurate event understanding. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to event extraction in social media that leverages cross-genre knowledge enrichment to improve the performance of event extraction. By incorporating knowledge from outside the social media text, such as Wikipedia, knowledge graphs, and web pages, we aim to provide a more comprehensive and accurate understanding of events. Our approach is based on the assumption that cross-genre knowledge can provide valuable context and depth to social media text, enabling event extractors to better identify the key elements of an event. To achieve this, we adopt a knowledge graph-based framework that integrates social media text with cross-genre knowledge. We create a graph that represents the events, entities, and relationships between them, and then use link prediction and entity disambiguation to enrich the event representation. By incorporating cross-genre knowledge, we enhance the event extraction capabilities of our system and demonstrate that it outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in terms of F-score improvement. Our contributions in this paper are two-fold. Firstly, we introduce a novel approach to event extraction in social media that leverages cross-genre knowledge enrichment. Our approach demonstrates that by integrating social media text with cross-genre knowledge, we can improve the performance of event extraction and provide a more comprehensive understanding of events. Secondly, we experimentally evaluate the effectiveness of our approach using a large-scale dataset of social media posts and achieve state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating the usefulness of knowledge enrichment in event extraction. With the increasing globalization of information exchange, texts in multilingual languages have become increasingly popular, particularly on the internet. A common type of multilingual text is the Chinese-English mixed text, where a few English words are embedded in a predominantly Chinese text. Examples of Chinese-English mixed texts can be found in modern Chinese articles, conversations, emails, and internet literature. However, part-of-speech tagging for such texts presents a significant challenge due to the difference in writing systems between Chinese and English. Chinese is a logograph-based language, where each character represents a word, while English is an alphabetic language, with each word represented by a sequence of alphabetic characters. As a result, existing POS tagging methods for Chinese are often inadequate for Chinese-English mixed texts. In the absence of a well-annotated corpus for Chinese-English mixed texts, most English words are simplified as "foreign words" (and treated as a certain type of "NOUN"), which loses important information about the word's POS and functionality within the sentence. In order to address this challenge, Hermann et al. (2015) have attempted to create a large-scale dataset of reading comprehension tasks. This data is based on summarised bullet points that have been paired with CNN and Daily Mail news articles, resulting in a corpus of over a million training examples. The creation of this dataset was a significant step forwards for the field of NLP, and marks an important point in the development of computer systems that can understand and interpret text. One of the key features of this dataset is that it is designed to assess the ability of a machine learning system to understand and comprehend the meaning of a passage of text, rather than simply relying on patterns and associations that may not be relevant to the task at hand. This is in contrast to many current NLP systems, which are often trained on datasets that are focused on very specific tasks, such as sentiment analysis or named entity recognition, rather than more general language understanding tasks like reading comprehension. Conversely, SS tasks often involve sparse and heterogeneous word distribution within a sentence, leading to a greater challenge in capturing the underlying semantic meaning. response: Linguistic alignment between dialogue partners has long been an intriguing phenomenon in the field of language and social interaction. A wealth of research has demonstrated that participants engage in various linguistic adaptations, such as adjustments in speech rate, pronunciation, and syntactic complexity, to negotiate and maintain social relationships (Brenneis and Macaulay, 1996; Erickson and Shulha, 2002). Recent studies have also contended that the power dynamics between interlocutors play a vital role in shaping linguistic alignment (Wolfram, 2006; Romero-Rodriguez et al., 2014). For instance, individuals in positions of higher power (e.g., employers, professionals) have been shown to exhibit more linguistic alignment with their counterparts, who are often found to be less assertive and less similar in terms of linguistic characteristics (Johnson, 2006). While this body of work has garnered significant attention, it often overlooks a critical aspect of language use: the pervasiveness of low-level linguistic features that can equally influence alignment. Variously known as low-level, high-frequency, or micro-features, these linguistic markers can comprise elementary building blocks such as word length, utterance duration, prosody, and phonological characteristics (Daly et al., 2004). Although some research has highlighted their importance in conversations (Hay ard, 2011), the majority of studies focused on the impact of social power have only subtly acknowledged, if not entirely disregarded, the potential effect of these low-level features (McGrath, 2013). This oversight might be attributed to the complexity of isolating the influence of individual low-level features, coupled with the pursuit of attributing the phenomenon to more higher-level constructs, such as social power and social status. In this paper, we revisit the assumption that interlocutors' social power is a primary determinant of the linguistic alignment between dialogue partners. To examine this issue, we employ logistic regression models to analyze two datasets and tease apart the unique contributions of both low-level linguistic features and social power to the observed alignment patterns. The first dataset includes conversations between speakers with varied levels of linguistic and social status, while the second dataset consists of free conversation data collected from a broader population. By carefully controlling for low-level features such as utterance length, syntactic complexity, and word order, we investigate whether the association between power and alignment diminishes, vanishes, or even inverts after accounting for these micro-structures. Our aim is not to completely dismiss the role of social power or even the idea that power differentially contributes to alignment under specific interactional conditions. Rather, we seek to more accurately characterize the relative impact of these confounding factors, particularly to clarify the causal relationship between linguistic structures, power dynamics, and conversational behavior. The deep auto-encoder (DAE) paradigm is one of the promising approaches, which has achieved state-of-the-art performance in various machine learning and natural language processing tasks (Bengio, 2013). DAE learns to reconstruct the input data by compressing it into a lower-dimensional representation and then decompressing it back into the original data. response: Argumentation and persuasion have been essential skills in human communication throughout history. Effective argumentation relies heavily on the ability to express opinions or make assertions supported by strong evidence. In recent years, argumentative writing has become increasingly important in various fields such as academic writing, politics, law, and business. Given the complexity and subjectivity of argumentative writing, finding competent and relevant supporting evidence can be challenging. One valuable source of supporting evidence is anecdotal information, which often provides a vivid and compelling narrative that helps to solidify a writer’s point or argument. Anecdotes, in this context, refer to brief, revealing stories or accounts that are often narratives of an individual person. While anecdotal information is widely used in various domains, there is a pressing need to develop systematic methods for identifying and recommending relevant anecdotes to support an argument or writing task. There are a few reasons why anecdote recognition and recommendation are important and timely. Firstly, the Internet and digital libraries have created vast repositories of text data containing anecdotes. However, manually sifting through this vast amount of text data to find relevant anecdotes can be very time-consuming, making it difficult for writers to find the evidence they need. Secondly, the unstructured and variable nature of anecdotal information makes it challenging to identify and find relevant anecdotes using traditional search methodologies. This is often compounded by the fact that many anecdotal accounts are buried in lengthy documents or buried in highly specific domains. Even with the rise of information retrieval systems such as search engines, the majority of anecdotal information remains archived and unaccessible. In this context, the development of systems that can automatically identify, understand, and recommend relevant anecdotes can greatly alleviate this challenge. This is precisely the motivation behind our work on Anecdote Recognition and Recommendation. ASNs are crucial to understanding virtually any substantial natural language text, and yet, their interpretation remains a largely unsolved problem. One of the primary obstacles in developing methods for automatically interpreting ASNs is the lack of annotated data. This is because annotating ASN interpretations requires manual expert knowledge and review, which can be time-consuming and expensive. We posit that ASNs can provide valuable insights and meaning to a sentence, but identifying this meaning is often arduous due to the absence of explicit data that demonstrates the relationship between the shell noun and its antecedent. As an example, consider the statement "I was aware of this fact." While "this fact" functions as a type of shell noun, with the noun "fact" playing the role of the antecedent, the content of "this fact" is not directly indicated in the sentence. Therefore, automatic methods have difficulty in determining the specific content of "this fact." Therefore, developing an accurate and efficient method to interpret ASNs is essential. The primary conjecture that underlies our approach is that the antecedents of cataphoric shell nouns (CSNs) can provide a rich and diverse dataset that can be exploited to improve the performance of ASN interpretation methods. CSNs have a clear construction that is structured around the antecedent, such that, in the example sentence "the reason that the engineer was fired was this issue," "this issue" is the antecedent, but its content, such as 'unfairness in the company's procedure,' can be identified through the antecedent ("the reason"). response: Introduction Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG) is a formalism that uses a logic-based syntax to generate tree structures, which makes it a powerful and expressive tool for modeling linguistic structure (Steedman, 2000). CCG has been successful in various NLP tasks, such as parsing, generation, and semantics (Clark and Curran, 2004; Clark et al., 2005; Bos, 2008). However, a major limitation of CCG is that it relies heavily on annotated resources, specifically treebanks, to train models. Creating and annotating large and wide-coverage treebanks for CCG is an expensive and time-consuming task, which hampers its applicability and adoption by the broader NLP community. In recent years, unsupervised parsing and grammar induction have emerged as promising alternatives to conventional supervised learning approaches, leveraging the abundance of plain texts available online and the advances in machine learning (Oepen, 2008; McDonald and Cram, 2012). Among various unsupervised parsing frameworks, Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG) induction is a particular attractive option, as it leverages the strengths of CCG's expressiveness and logic-based syntax. Yet, despite these advances, current CCG induction methodologies still face several challenges. Firstly, most existing CCG induction approaches rely on surface-level linguistic features or statistical patterns, which may not capture the deeper, underlying semantic and syntactic structures of language. Secondly, the resulting induced grammars are often over-specified and lack generalizability across different domains, such as in terms of shared linguistic patterns and structures. Finally, the current lack of effective evaluation metrics and supervised modeling architectures limits the overall performance and interpretability of induced CCG models. In this paper, we address these limitations by proposing a novel unsupervised CCG induction approach, which consists of two main innovations. Firstly, we incorporate boundary part-of-speech (POS) tags into the model, recognizing that lexical information plays a crucial role in forming the structural relationships between words. By utilizing boundary POS tags, our model can effectively capture the unique properties of individual words and grammatical patterns within a sentence. Secondly, we implement a nonparametric Bayesian inference framework using the Pitman-Yor process, which enables the model to learn compact and generalized grammars. This Bayesian approach allows our model to capture the variability and uncertainty inherent in linguistic data, leading to more robust and accurate CCG induction. We conduct experiments on the English Penn treebank to evaluate the effectiveness of our innovations, demonstrating that incorporating boundary POS tags and using Bayesian learning significantly improves the grammatical structure and semantics of the induced CCG models. However, the task becomes increasingly challenging when faced with dynamic sentiment ambiguous adjectives (DSAAs) - a set of adjectives whose meaning and sentiment orientation change dynamically depending on the context. Examples of DSAAs include "large," "small," "high," and "low," which can both be positive or negative depending on the situation (e.g., "large" is typically positive when describing a house, but negative when describing a financial loss). Given the complexities involved, traditional sentiment analysis methods, which often rely on pre-trained models or hand-crafted rules, may struggle to accurately capture the nuances of DSAAs. A more promising approach is to revisit the problem from a knowledge-based perspective. Rather than relying on general-purpose sentiment lexicons or machine learning models, our approach focuses on the co-occurrence of adjectives with target nouns to infer their sentiment expectation. We propose to frame this as a sentiment classification task, where the goal is to predict the sentiment of target nouns rather than the adjectives themselves. This shift in focus allows us to leverage the power of linguistic patterns and word senses, avoiding the noisy and often ambiguous semantics associated with certain sentiment lexicons. Our approach is grounded in the insights from linguistic theory, which suggests that the meaning of words is composed of multiple components, such as their lexical, grammatical, and pragmatic aspects. By analyzing the co-occurrence patterns of adjectives and target nouns, we can infer the sentiment expectation associated with these nouns. To this end, we design a framework that leverages the following key components: First, we employ a lexico-syntactic pattern mining technique to extract sentiment expectation features from a large corpus of text. Traditional summarization methods, however, often concentrate on selecting the most salient sentences or keywords from the source texts without group-ing sentences that share strong semantic relationships, making the generated summaries less coherent (Arndt et al., 2005). A coherent summary is one that covers the various aspects and views of a topic presented in the source texts, connecting these views and making the text more readable and understandable (Goldstein, 1997). One such human-based approach is crowdsourcing, which leverages a large and diverse pool of individuals to collect and annotate data. In particular, microtasking platforms, such as Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT), provide a convenient and cost-effective way to collect annotations from "Turkers" (workers on AMT). However, the quality and accuracy of crowdsourced data can be compromised by various factors, including worker biases and variability in annotation behavior. This raises the question of whether crowdsourcing is a suitable approach for certain NLP tasks, such as query segmentation, which requires precise and consistent annotations. Query segmentation, also known as query chunking, is a fundamental step towards query understanding and satisfaction, enabling search systems to identify relevant information and provide accurate search results. response: The quest for a massive, multilingual dictionary has driven the development of various translation technologies for decades, notably with the emergence of machine translation and translation memory. Recently, the rise of user generated content on the internet has led to a proliferation of dictionaries, notably Wiktionaries 1 and translation dictionaries 2, that have significantly expanded the size and scope of bilingual and multilingual dictionaries. Today, researchers and practitioners seek to benefit from the collective work of these efforts by compiling a large set of bilingual or multilingual dictionaries in order to increase coverage, consistency, and accessibility to knowledge across languages. To this end, we explore the use of probabilistic inference to compile a massive, multilingual dictionary that is larger than any one of its constituent dictionaries by aggregating the word translations from various bilingual dictionaries and Wiktionaries. Our problem addresses the longstanding issues with word translation in language processing by integrating the translation information over multiple language pairs, and by avoiding the limitations of a single translation dictionary, which does not allow us to take advantage of the transitive relation among translations. For example, if word A is translated to word B in one translation dictionary, and word B is then translated to word C in another relevant language dictionary, the translation of A to C is not exhibited in the collection of available translation dictionaries. This is the intrinsic problem we call the transitive inference problem. We solved this transitive inference problem by leveraging probabilistic logic for reasoning about uncertainty in the source, and target languages, that relate the translations of a word in multiple bilingual dictionaries through multilingual dictionaries. This paper presents a scalable method for probabilistically compiling such massive, multilingual dictionaries using first-order probabilistic logic programming. We introduce the world's largest collaborative multilingual dictionary that aggregates the translations from over 1,000 languages, with a total of over 10,000,000 word translations. We show that our aggregation of dictionaries, consists of: Wiktionaries with 8 million words and 1.4 million translations and 242 translation dictionaries each containing on average 100,000 words for 200 languages, runs in constant memory usage (about 50 GB for a 64 bit architecture) even on commodity hardware. response: Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) is a central task in natural language processing (NLP), serving as a fundamental component for numerous downstream applications, such as question answering, sentiment analysis, and text summarization. Assessing the semantic similarity between two texts has been an active research area, with hundreds of STS systems developed to date. While designers of NLP systems aim to leverage existing STS systems, the crucial question of which system is best suited for a particular task remains unresolved. To address this challenge, intrinsic evaluation is typically conducted by comparing the STS system's output against human judgments on semantic similarity. The use of Pearson correlation as the primary metric for intrinsic evaluation has become widespread, allowing designers to estimate how well a particular STS system aligns with human judgments. However, this study underscores a critical problem: relying on intrinsic evaluations using Pearson correlation can be misleading, especially when conducting evaluations in downstream tasks that rely on STS. This result highlights the importance of evaluating the STS systems more thoroughly, rather than solely relying on a hypothetical "coverage" in terms of the Pearson correlation between human and system judgments, to select the best performaning metric. Through three examples of relevant downstream tasks, this work demonstrates that various evaluation measures other than Pearson correlation, which have been less frequently used in the intrinsic evaluation setting, can elucidate inconsistencies in the quality of the STS systems. These examples critique the restrictions of employing Pearson correlation as the only metric and show that relying solely on its value may lead to selecting an inadequate STS system for the task at hand. Moreover, they emphasize the necessity for an awareness of the task's requirements and applicability. Therefore, it is essential to outline how to assess the validity of an intrinsic evaluation. Understanding the task's properties and selecting the adequate intrinsic metrics for evaluation form the core of our proposed framework. This framework is particularly designed to address the pitfalls of using Pearson correlation as the sole metric for intrinsic evaluation. In an attempt to address these limitations and arrive at a more accurate selection of the STS best performing metric, we discuss key task-specific characteristics that can influence the choice of metrics to be used in intrinsic evaluation. As a result, we offer a framework for conducting intrinsic evaluation that incorporates the properties of the task at hand to offer a more comprehensive assessment of the quality of the STS system. Our findings suggest that task-oriented intrinsic evaluation that accounts for task-specific factors provides the most accurate insights into the suitability of STS systems for particular applications. This contributes to refining the field of STS, enabling NLP designers to make more informed decisions when selecting STS systems for downstream tasks. This framework thereby addresses the inherent limitation of prior work, where intrinsic evaluation is often seen as a generic tool. It is pertinent to note, however, that future work involves a holistic view of intrinsic evaluation to consider newly emerging methods. Additionally, generalization of our results to downstream tasks beyond the tested applications remains a valuable direction of study. A key challenge in text analysis is the need to model and represent the inherent complexity of human language, where a single word, phrase, or passage may convey meaning in multiple ways. Latent Variable Models (LVMs) of Text, a family of probabilistic models that involve unobserved or latent variables (Arora et al., 2012;Ghahramani, 2015;Welling et al., 2005;Ytreberg et al., 2018), provide a particularly appealing solution to this challenge. However, the benefits of adopting LVMs for text analysis come at a computational cost, which has grown more pronounced in recent years due to the increasing size of text corpora and desire to train more powerful models (Li et al., 2016). Websites like Yahoo! Answers, Quora, and Zhihu have over a billion registered users worldwide, demonstrating the immense potential of CQA in disseminating information and expertise. CQA systems typically group questions and their corresponding answers together to provide users with a convenient platform to seek and provide information. Answer selection, however, poses a formidable challenge as it involves selecting the most relevant and accurate answer from a large pool of candidate answers. In spite of its importance, answer selection remains understudied in the field of CQA. Traditional approaches to answer selection often rely on shallow features such as TF-IDF or the anchor text of hyperlinks within the question and answer text, without considering the unique structural characteristics of CQA questions. Specifically, a real-world CQA forum often presents questions as two interrelated components: a subject that summarizes the main points of the question, and a body that elaborates on the subject in detail. Although these two components are closely linked, prior research on answer selection frequently ignores the subject-body relationship, treating the question as a single, concatenated representation. Ignoring the subject-body relationship may lead to neglecting vital information within the CQA question. The subject typically provides a clear, high-level overview of the query, while the body offers more nuanced details that can be crucial in understanding the context of the question. Recent advances in deep learning have shown promise in modeling complex document representations that capture long-range dependencies and context-specific relationships within text. However, such techniques have yet to be employed in CQA systems to fully leverage the structural information of CQA questions. response: The Standardization of Named Entities: Challenges and Opportunities Extracting and representing named entities in text is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), with far-reaching implications for information retrieval, question answering, text summarization, and other applications. However, one of the most significant challenges in working with named entities lies in their inherent variability in representation, making it difficult to compare, aggregate, and reason about entities effectively. For instance, the same individual or organization may be referred to using multiple names, such as "John F. Kennedy," "JFK," or "President Kennedy," due to differences in context, style, or language. The lack of standardization in representing named entities can result in a myriad of issues, including entity duplication, inconsistencies, and inaccuracies, ultimately hindering the reliability and effectiveness of NLP systems. In recent years, the canonicalization of named entities has gained significant attention as a means of resolving these discrepancies and providing a unified representation of entities across different contexts and attributes. Canonicalization involves transforming named entity mentions into a standardized format that exposes their underlying attributes, such as names, titles, locations, and dates. The resulting representation can facilitate more accurate and robust NLP applications, including named entity recognition (NER), entity linking (EL), and relation extraction. A key aspect of entity canonicalization is the determination of entity attributes, which represent the underlying properties or aspects of an entity. Traditional approaches to attribute extraction focus on predefined, hand-crafted rules or machine learning algorithms that rely on manually annotated data to learn attribute patterns. However, these methods often suffer from limitations, such as the need for extensive human resources, time-consuming annotation processes, and the difficulty of capturing complex attribute dependencies. To address these challenges, we turn to statistical models and machine learning techniques, which can provide a more systematic and scalable approach to entity canonicalization. A promising direction is the use of Bayesian inference and transductive learning to combine knowledge about entity context, surface features, and attribute-part dependencies. By incorporating these factors, a probabilistic model can learn to represent entities as tables whose rows correspond to entities and whose columns are attributes or parts thereof. This representation enables more effective entity aggregation, comparison, and reasoning, ultimately leading to improved NLP performance. In this paper, we introduce a novel probabilistic model for canonicalizing named entity mentions, incorporating entity context, surface features, first-order dependencies among attribute-parts, and a notion of noise. Our approach employs transductive learning from a few seeds and a collection of mention tokens, combining Bayesian inference and conditional estimation. We evaluate the model and its components on two datasets collected from political blogs and sports news, demonstrating its effectiveness and outperformance of a simple agglomerative clustering approach and previous work. By addressing the challenges of entity canonicalization through a probabilistic model, we aim to contribute to the development of more robust and accurate NLP systems that can effectively handle the complexities of named entities. response: Relation extraction is a critical task in natural language processing (NLP), with applications in information extraction, question answering, and text summarization, among others. It typically involves identifying entities and their associated relationships from text. Traditional relation extraction approaches rely on hand-engineered features, including part-of-speech tags, named entity recognition (NER) results, group phrase chunks, and dependency parses. However, these methods require extensive domain knowledge and are often inadequate for handling out-of-vocabulary words or entity ambiguity. Moreover, extracting complex relational structures between entities using these approaches can be cumbersome, time-consuming, and error-prone. Recent advances in deep learning have led to the development of robust neural network architectures, notably using recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and long short-term memory networks (LSTMs), that have shown impressive performance in sequence classification and tagging tasks. Building upon these successes, this study aims to develop an end-to-end neural model that combines the strengths of sequential LSTMs and tree-structured LSTMs for relation extraction. Our proposed model distinguishes itself from previous attempts, leveraging the bidirectional LSTM-RNN to model sequential word dependencies and the tree-structured LSTM-RNN to capture the hierarchical, sub-tree structure of entity relationships. By learning from these two complementary representations in a multi-task setting, our model enables shared learning of entity detection and relation classification. Understanding how words are composed and how they convey meaning has been an area of interest for linguists and natural language processing researchers alike for decades. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the study of compositional semantics, the process by which the meaning of an expression is derived from the meaning of its parts (Barsalou, 2003;Fodor, 1975). This has led to the development of various computational models of compositional meaning, which aim to capture the way in which words are combined to form more complex expressions. One domain that offers a unique testbed for studying compositional semantics is the study of compounds, words that are formed by combining two or more free morphemes into a single unit (G jets, 1979). The semantic properties of German compounds have been extensively described in linguistic literature (Ackerman and Webelhuth, 1999), providing a rich source of data for the evaluation and development of computational models of compositional meaning. Recently, the advent of large-scale linguistic resources and the emergence of deep learning-based techniques have enabled researchers to approach the problem of compositional semantics through the lens of vector space models (VSMs) (Bengio et al., 2003). With the rapid growth of online reviews and user-generated content, there has been a pressing need for accurate and fine-grained analysis of semantic orientation at the sentence level. Most existing approaches to sentence-level semantic orientation analysis focus on predicting the polarity (positive or negative) of opinions, which is often referred to as opinion polarity analysis. However, a deeper understanding of user opinions can be obtained by analyzing not only the polarity but also the strength of opinions expressed. Opinion strength refers to the intensity or magnitude of opinions, which is often neglected in prior research. Predicting both opinion polarity and strength at the level of individual sentences is challenging due to the lack of sentence-level training data for both aspects. Most existing datasets only provide document-level ratings or coarser-grained annotations, which does not allow for effective training of models for fine-grained analysis. For example, in movie review datasets, the average rating at the document level can mask subtle differences in opinions expressed in different sentences. Given these challenges, it is essential to develop robust and reliable methods for sentence-level semantic orientation analysis that can accurately predict both opinion polarity and strength. In this paper, we propose the Weakly Supervised Multi-Experts Model (MEM) for sentence-level semantic orientation analysis. MEM is designed to cope with the lack of sentence-level training data by leveraging weak supervision signals from coarse-grained training data, a small set of diverse base predictors, and, if available, fine-grained training data. One critical challenge for developing these applications is finding an adequate semantic interpretation of natural language constructs. response: Word representation learning has been a crucial area of research in natural language processing (NLP) and artificial intelligence. Most word representation learning methods rely on the distributional hypothesis, which states that words that are used and occur in the same contexts tend to possess similar meanings. These methods are based on the assumption that words with similar meanings will tend to appear in similar contexts and use similar words. This distributional approach has been successful in representing words in various tasks such as language modeling, sentiment analysis, and named entity recognition. However, there exist some limitations in these methods. The distributional approach to word representation tends to confuse the concept of meaning and cooccurrence of words. This often results in emotional dissimilar words possessing similar word representations. For instance, the words "happy" and "sad" often appear in similar contexts, such as in sentences with subjects expressing a personal experience. Consequently, the distributional methods tend to assign similar word representations to the words "happy" and "sad", even though they have opposite emotional meanings. Moreover, words with similar emotional meanings such as "happy" and "joy" may end up being assigned dissimilar word representations due to their different cooccurrence frequencies. This oversight often results in poor performance in tasks that require an understanding of emotional states, such as emotion classification and emotion similarity. Another issue with the current word representation learning methods is their inability to capture the nuances of emotional language. Emotions are complex and can only be implicitly conveyed through the language used. Traditional word representation learning methods fail to account for these subtle variations in emotional language. Therefore, they end up masking the true emotional connotations of words in their representations. To address these limitations, a new approach to word representation learning has been proposed. This is a novel method of obtaining emotion-enriched word representations, which projects emotionally similar words into neighboring spaces and emotionally dissimilar ones far apart. The proposed approach leverages distant supervision to automatically obtain a large training dataset of text documents. Two recurrent neural network architectures are designed to learn the emotion-enriched representations. The first architecture is designed to model the causal relationships between words and their cooccurrence within a text. The second architecture is designed to model the affective relationships between words, including the emotional nuances that are embedded in language. Our intention is to leverage the strengths of both architectures to capture the complex relationships between words, which give us richer word representations. Our method captures the subtle variations of emotional language by evaluating the relationships between words at multiple levels of granularity. By refining the through the sentiment of the complete sentences in the corpus, the proposed approach contributes to improved predictions in tasks that relate to affect, such as emotion classification and emotion similarity. Our benchmarks for comparison consist of a collection of general-purpose word representations, including word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and glove (Pennington et al., 2014), as well as some of the more recent affective word representations. response: Sentiment classification in online review platforms has become increasingly important with the growth of e-commerce. Although deep learning-based methods have made remarkable improvements in sentiment analysis, they usually rely on prior knowledge about the users and products being reviewed, which may not be available for new users and products. This is particularly true in scenarios with limited training data, an issue commonly referred to as the "cold-start" problem. Most existing approaches ignoring the cold-start problem assume that all users and products have a sufficient number of reviews to train an effective model. However, in real-world scenarios, it is not uncommon to encounter new users and products with very limited data. For instance, when an e-commerce company starts a new service or launches a new product, there will be no or very few reviews about it. The lack of sufficient data makes it challenging for existing models to handle the sentiment analysis task effectively. In this study, we focus on addressing the cold-start problem in sentiment classification. We introduce a new framework, called Hybrid Contextualized Sentiment Classifier (HCSC), which comprises two key modules: a fast word encoder and a novel attention mechanism called Cold-Start Aware Attention (CSAA). The word encoder module is responsible for extracting contextualized word representations from raw text data. It leverages a design to incorporate both short- and long-range dependency features in word embeddings, which captures richer semantic information in text. The CSAA module takes the encoded word vectors as input and adaptively decides whether to use shared vectors constructed from similar users or products when these are cold-start cases. This module is crucial in handling the cold-start problem and was originally solved using shared vectors which were constructed from similar entities but it made HCSC significantly more complex. In addition, a frequency-guided selective gate vector is proposed to decide whether to employ the shared vectors in cases where the original distinct vectors lack sufficient information. This design effectively balances the trade-off between handling the cold-start problem and maintaining model complexity. Several previous models were proposed to address the sentiment classification task but they failed to address the cold-start problem. One such example is (Zhou et al., 2017), where the authors utilized an embedding space to integrate user and product information, but it did not adequately deal with cold-start cases. In contrast to (Zhou et al., 2017), this research assess the impact of the cold-start problem more accurately, showing better performance with a much simpler model than existing state-of-the-art methods (often trained under very diverse settings). Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed HCSC model enhances sentiment classification performance, especially when training data is limited and the cold-start problem is present. Moreover, the model's simplicity allows it to be trained much faster than complex alternative approaches that achieved state-of-the-art accuracy under other settings. These results indicate that HCSC is not only accurate but also practical and deployable in real-world scenarios. response: Social media platforms like Twitter have been growing exponentially since their inception, with over 440 million tweets being sent every day (Kwak et al., 2010). The ever-increasing amount of user-generated content poses challenges for both humans and machines, particularly when it comes to processing, analyzing, and summarizing Twitter conversations. Unlike traditional news articles or web pages, online social media platforms lack the inherent structure that comes with more formal writing. Consequently, users post short messages (typically no longer than 280 characters) with varying degrees of coherence, making it difficult to grasp the underlying content. In response to the pressing need for data summarization in social media research (Qazvinian et al., 2009), previous studies have experimented with different summarization techniques such as tweets selection and aggregation (G jetsanjani et al., 2017) or automatic content analysis, to name but a few. Nonetheless, and as of today, there exist very limited methods for providing a concise and meaningful summary of the topics being discussed on Twitter. Summarizing Twitter in terms of topical keyphrases is more relevant, as mainstream summarization approaches perform poorly in automatic summarization on social media platforms (Kumar, 2014). Topical keyphrases can offer a clear snapshot of the main topics discussed in a tweet, as well as provide context about the events and opinions unfolding in the Twitter sphere. However, keyphrase extraction from Twitter posts poses unique challenges, particularly due to: i) the short length of tweets; ii) lack of although straightforwardness found in traditional data; iii) the colloquial nature of age-generation in social media platforms. Traditional single document summarization methods typically rely on well-structured documents that contain the explicit information that the summarizer targets. However, when working with micro-posts in social media, keyphrases identification must take into account the low-level of text formation available, i.e., short phrases found in singular tweets. To surpass the limitation that the highly fragmentary structure of Twitter engenders, traditional techniques for text summarization fall short. The reason is that these methods necessitate cohesiveness within the targeted content. This calls for the need of alternative methods for summarizing Twitter content that need to take alternative pervasive and highly agespecific characteristics into account. Recent efforts have highlighted both the quantity and quality problems prevalent in the areas of summarizing and analyzing tweets (Qazvinian et al., 2009), alongside evaluations of pre-existing based summarization techniques. However, tokenization can be quite challenging for certain languages such as Chinese and Korean due to their complex orthography and writing systems. Traditionally, tokenization is done as a first step, followed by translation, where the translation system relies on the 1-best tokenization of the source sentence. However, tokenization errors can still introduce translation mistakes even when using state-of-the-art machine translation systems. To alleviate this problem, traditional approaches rely on generating lattices that contain multiple possible tokenizations of the source sentence. While these solutions have shown promise and flexibility, they are inherently more complex and computationally expensive due to the need to parse and re-score the lattice during translation.
